description: Hand-curated modal oracle. Covers Dorian (#6), Mixolydian (b7), Phrygian (bII), Lydian (#4), Aeolian (pure natural minor), and modal-vs-functional negative controls. Each case has music-theory rationale; expected values written from theory, not generated from analyzer behavior.
schema_notes: Most cases pass key_hint to isolate modal-detection logic from the major-mode key-detection bug (task #8).
Cases that intentionally test ambiguity (negative controls, too-short cases) deliberately omit key_hint and use mode_must_not_be to assert the analyzer doesn't over-commit.

Where a case uses CHORDS WITHOUT 7THS, that's deliberate — the analyzer's mode-signature matcher does exact-token comparison, so 'IV7' or 'bIImaj7' tokens don't match the bare 'IV' / '♭II' signatures. Cases needing modal classification keep chords as bare triads.

progressions.name: d_dorian_i_IV_classic
progressions.comment: Textbook Dorian vamp. G major contains B-natural — that's the raised 6th, the Dorian signature against natural minor (which has B♭). The major IV chord IS the distinguishing feature; if classified as Aeolian/minor, that's wrong.

progressions.name: e_dorian_i_IV_classic
progressions.comment: Same shape transposed to E. A major contains C♯ — the Dorian #6 in E. Confirms Dorian detection isn't D-specific.

progressions.name: d_dorian_with_minor_v
progressions.comment: Dorian with the natural-minor v (Am, no leading tone). Important: the v stays MINOR (lowercase) — Dorian doesn't raise the 7th. The IV major is what makes it Dorian, not the v.

progressions.name: a_dorian_iv_then_IV_juxtaposition
progressions.comment: The piece de resistance: minor iv (Dm) and major IV (D) side by side. The IV chord with F♯ is the Dorian raised 6; the iv with F-natural is the natural-minor 6. Real music does this — same scale degree, different quality. Analyzer should commit to Dorian on the strength of the major IV.

progressions.name: d_mixolydian_bVII_drone
progressions.comment: Classic Mixolydian: I-♭VII-IV-I. C major has C-natural, the lowered 7th of D — the Mixolydian signature against D major's leading-tone C♯.

progressions.name: a_mixolydian_southern_rock
progressions.comment: Same shape, A tonic. G major has G-natural = ♭7 of A. The classic 'Sweet Home Alabama' / 'Cinnamon Girl' / Southern-rock Mixolydian color.

progressions.name: g_mixolydian_simple_vamp
progressions.comment: Two-chord vamp showing Mixolydian needs only the ♭VII to read. The IV chord isn't required for classification, just the ♭7 above the tonic.

progressions.name: e_phrygian_bII_signature
progressions.comment: Phrygian's distinguishing chord: a major triad on the lowered 2nd. F major over E tonic gives the half-step-above-tonic flavor that's instantly recognizable as Phrygian (Spanish/flamenco color).

progressions.name: b_phrygian_bII_alternation
progressions.comment: Same Phrygian shape, B tonic. C major over B is the bII. Confirms detection is tonic-agnostic.

progressions.name: c_lydian_attempt_documents_gap
progressions.comment: EXPECTED-FAIL bug ticket: D major in C contains F♯ — the Lydian #4. But the analyzer's Lydian signature looks for '♯IV' or '♭V' tokens; this progression produces 'II' instead. The pitch evidence IS Lydian, but the current signature matcher misses it. This case documents that gap — the right fix is teaching the matcher that 'II' (a major chord on the natural 2nd) over a major tonic IS a Lydian indicator (it implies #4 in the chord). Until then, this fails.

progressions.name: f_lydian_attempt_documents_gap
progressions.comment: EXPECTED-FAIL: same Lydian-detection gap as previous, F tonic. G major contains B-natural = #4 of F. The pitch evidence is unambiguous Lydian. Two failing cases on the same gap make the bug ticket harder to ignore.

progressions.name: b_aeolian_pure_natural_minor_documents_dorian_misfire
progressions.comment: EXPECTED-FAIL bug ticket. Chord pitches are pure B Aeolian (B C♯ D E F♯ G A — no G♯ which would be Dorian's raised 6). But the analyzer reports 'B Dorian' because the Dorian signature ['VI', '♯VI', 'II', 'IV'] matches the bare 'VI' token in the romans. The 'VI' here is the codebase's label for the chord on natural ♭6 (G in B minor) — but the Dorian matcher reads it as raised-6 evidence. This is the concrete functional consequence of the convention ambiguity tracked in task #9: 'VI' (without ♭) is overloaded across modes. Fix is either (a) emit '♭VI' at slot 8 (cascades into other oracle cases), or (b) make the Dorian matcher check actual chord pitches, not just roman tokens. Either fix would unblock this case.

progressions.name: modal_too_short_to_commit
progressions.comment: Just i-iv-i. No mode-characteristic notes (Am has C-natural and E, both ambiguous between Aeolian and Phrygian; F-natural absent rules out Lydian/major; C♯ absent rules out Dorian; etc.). The analyzer must NOT over-commit. Aeolian or None are both fine; anything else is a false positive.

progressions.name: major_with_borrowed_iv_not_modal
progressions.comment: Modal mixture, NOT a mode change. The minor iv (Fm with A♭) is borrowed from C minor — a textbook chromatic color in major-key tonal music. Should NOT classify as Dorian (which has the OPPOSITE: major IV in a minor key). The presence of MAJOR IV first establishes the major-key context; the brief minor iv is decoration.

progressions.name: brief_dorian_color_in_minor
progressions.comment: Three chords, raised 6 (D major has F♯, the raised 6 of A natural minor). Even a brief major-IV gesture committee to Dorian — the F♯ is unambiguous. If the analyzer demands more evidence than this, the threshold is too high.
